title: The mind like the wind
hook: Arjuna says the mind can't be held; Krishna says practice and letting go can hold it
carry: abhyasa and vairagya: the self lifts the self
tomorrow: maya: illusion, or God's real power? who's right?

segments.voice: Yesterday: aham, I; tvam, you; ime, these; vayam, we. And Krishna's first teaching: the atman was never born and never dies.

Halfway through the Gita's sixth chapter, Arjuna pushes back. Krishna has been teaching him to sit and steady the mind, and Arjuna says, more or less: I can't. The mind is restless, stubborn, strong; holding it is as hard as holding the wind. Krishna doesn't argue. He agrees. And earlier in that same chapter, he'd given a verse that seems stuck on one word: uddhared atmanatmanam. Atman, atman, atman. Why say self over and over?
screen: `THE MIND IS LIKE THE WIND.` → `KRISHNA AGREES.` → `ATMAN, ATMAN, ATMAN.`

segments.voice: The answer is the word itself. Atman can mean the self in the big sense, or plain oneself, the way English says himself or herself, and this verse, Gita 6.5, uses both. Uddhared atmanatmanam, natmanam avasadayet; atmaiva hy atmano bandhur, atmaiva ripur atmanah. Let one lift the self by the self, and not sink the self; for the self alone is the self's friend, and the self alone its enemy. Bandhu, friend, also kin. Ripu, enemy. The endings tell the shapes apart: atmana, by the self; atmanam, the self being lifted; atmanah, of the self. The next verse explains: to one who has mastered himself, the self is a friend; to one who hasn't, it behaves like an enemy. Now the teaching, and this is Hindu yoga at its root. When Arjuna says the mind is like the wind, Krishna answers: abhyasena tu kaunteya vairagyena cha grihyate. It is held by abhyasa and by vairagya. Abhyasa, practice: coming back, again and again, to the chosen thing, a mantra, the breath, the name of God. Vairagya: loosening the grip of wanting. That pair is the backbone of Hindu meditation; Patanjali's Yoga Sutras name the very same two. So Gita 6.5 isn't a pep talk. It's a discipline. The self lifts the self by returning, day after day, and the same word stands at both ends of the rope.
screen: `ATMAN: THE SELF, OR ONESELF.` · `LIFT THE SELF BY THE SELF.` · `FRIEND OR ENEMY OF ITSELF.` · `ABHYASA AND VAIRAGYA.` · then, large: `THE SAME WORD AT BOTH ENDS OF THE ROPE.`

segments.voice: Do what Krishna prescribes, in small. Choose one anchor: Om, or a mantra you know, like Om namah Shivaya, or the name of God you pray to; if you don't pray, your own breath. Repeat it softly. Each time the mind runs off, and it will, that's the wind. Come back without scolding. Each return is abhyasa.
Two hundred core words: today, atman, the self, or plain oneself, in its shapes atma, atmanam, atmana, atmanah. And two that hold it steady: abhyasa, practice, and vairagya, letting go.
The line to take with you: abhyasa and vairagya. The self lifts the self by coming back, again and again.

howItsDone: Many Hindus practice japa, repeating a mantra or a name of God, often on a mala of 108 beads, and simply come back to it when the mind wanders; some learn Gita 6.5 by heart.
